newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds still surging up on foreign buying.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds still surging up on foreign buying.

text.p: Irish bonds continued to surge higher in active trade on Friday, boosted by further foreign buying as well as a well-subscribed tap issue and Thursday's positive Irish inflation data, dealers said.

"There is renewed foreign interest in the market. After the tap and inflation figures, bonds are looking very healthy at the moment, especially the ten-year which has galloped ahead in the last few days," one dealer said.
By 1500 GMT the eight percent bond due 2001 was up 39p at 104.85 to yield 6.50 percent while the eight percent bond due 2006 was up 90p at 104.90 to yield 7.16 percent.
The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) held a 100 million punt tap issue in the eight percent bond due 2006, and dealers said it was well-subscribed.

Dealers said foreign buying on EMU convergence trades was pushing the market higher. The market was also helped by Thursday's benign CPI inflation data and central bank comments that short-term inflation would stay low, they said.
"There's some convergence going on in European markets and Ireland is sharing in that," Riada economist Padhraic Garvey said.
"There has been concern that credit numbers are growing too strongly, but the fact that the inflation figures were so low has muted some of those concerns," he said.

Despite the central bank's upbeat comments on short-term inflation, it warned that "the medium term outlook looks less promising", and said Ireland's strong credit growth remained a cause for concern.
"Financial markets will be watching inflation and credit growth data very carefully for the next few months," Garvey said.
